title: Paleogenomics and habitat modeling reveal temperate Eurasian origins of woolly rhinoceroses.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Listed all 284 entries in the Zenodo archive by a ranged read of the zip central directory (no full download: the zip is 92 MB, over the 50 MB cap), then pulled and decompressed README.md, MANIFEST.md, run_all_Fig3.m and Fig3_CDE.m by ranged requests. Exactly one data file exists: HABITATc_Cantiquitatis_S7_matPredictors_05x_500kya.nc, 519,460,377 bytes uncompressed. Its README states it holds a single variable, ANTIQUITATIS = habitat suitability on a 0 to 1 scale, 'derived from a Mahalanobis distance-based model', global 0.5 degree grid, last 500,000 years at 1,000-year steps; the byte count matches 720 x 360 x 501 four-byte floats exactly. Everything else in the archive is MATLAB plotting code (the third-party m_map mapping toolbox) and three output PDF panels. Licence MIT, no login. Also queried Europe PMC (no full text, no supplementary files, no cross-references, no text-mined accessions), the European Nucleotide Archive, and NCBI BioProject for Coelodonta (6 hits, none matching this paper's 14 nuclear + 29 mitochondrial genomes).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The specimen counts (183 fossils screened, 29 mitochondrial and 14 nuclear genomes recovered), the geographic spread and the dating all come from the abstract and press coverage. The paper is paywalled with no PubMed Central copy, so I never saw the supplementary specimen tables, the fossil occurrence coordinates, or the climate predictor variables that fed the habitat model.

a1_downloadable.note: The Zenodo archive is openly downloadable under the MIT licence with no login, confirmed by a successful ranged HTTP request. The DNA sequence data accession, however, could not be located anywhere: Europe PMC reports no cross-references and no text-mined accessions, and no matching project exists in the European Nucleotide Archive or NCBI BioProject.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: There is no measured outcome column anywhere in the deposit. The fossil occurrence records (where and when a woolly rhinoceros was actually found), the specimen metadata and the radiocarbon dates are not included; they sit in supplementary tables behind the Science paywall. Any prediction target would have to be built from scratch out of external fossil databases.

a3_inputs_present.note: The file name says 'matPredictors', but the predictor variables themselves are absent. The NetCDF file carries only three coordinate arrays (longitude, latitude, time) and the single output variable, confirmed by reading the plotting script's ncread calls. The paleoclimate inputs would have to be regenerated from an external climate emulator the paper does not deposit.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are clear and documented: habitat suitability on a 0 to 1 scale, degrees longitude and latitude, time in thousands of years before present. Stated in README.md, which I read.

a5_enough_rows.note: The biological unit is the specimen, and there are at most 43 of them (29 mitochondrial plus 14 nuclear genomes, from 183 fossils screened) against a checklist floor of 400 for classification. The 93 million grid cells in the NetCDF file are not independent observations; they are one model's smooth output over a map, where neighbouring cells are near-identical by construction.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 0.52 GB NetCDF, read one time slice at a time
a6_fits_laptop.note: Comfortably laptop-sized: a 519 MB array that standard NetCDF tools read slice by slice, so peak memory stays near 2 GB. No graphics card needed. This is the only Part A item the data passes easily.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: What I could cross-check lines up: the file's byte count is exactly 720 x 360 x 501 four-byte values, matching the README's stated 0.5 degree global grid over 500,000 years at 1,000-year steps. The specimen counts could not be checked against any file.

a8_label_provenance.note: The only quantity in the deposit is the output of the authors' own Mahalanobis-distance habitat model, computed from climate predictors. Training anything to predict it from climate would be copying their model's arithmetic, not learning biology, and the score would be high for a reason that means nothing. This is textbook circularity plus leakage by construction.

existing_models.name: The paper's own Mahalanobis distance habitat model (a classical statistical measure of how unusual a site's climate is compared with sites where the species is known to have lived)
existing_models.score_and_split: No predictive accuracy is reported anywhere I could see; the deposit contains the fitted output grid and plotting code only, with no held-out evaluation, no area-under-the-curve figure and no cross-validation.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrievable: the paper is paywalled with no PubMed Central copy, so I could not read the discussion.

existing_models.name: Maxent (a widely used maximum-entropy species distribution model) as applied to extinct Pleistocene megafauna
existing_models.score_and_split: Search returned published applications to Pleistocene rewilding proxies and to extinct South American megafauna (Equus neogeus, Notiomastodon platensis), but I retrieved titles and snippets only, so I am not citing any accuracy number.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not established; I did not retrieve the full texts.

existing_models.name: Deep-learning species distribution models (convolutional neural networks and vision transformers over climate raster layers)
existing_models.score_and_split: A 2026 Global Ecology and Biogeography benchmark (Kellenberger et al.) reports from its abstract that deep learning matches but does not surpass existing methods on average, and is substantially worse for species with narrow ranges and few data points. Title and abstract snippet retrieved via search; full text not read.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Performance for rare species with few occurrence records, which is exactly the woolly rhinoceros situation.

integration.partner_dataset: Considered and rejected: the Neotoma Paleoecology Database and the Stage 3 Project / Lorenzen et al. radiocarbon compilations of Eurasian megafauna occurrences would be the natural partners for fossil locality records.
integration.join_key: Latitude, longitude and calibrated age in thousands of years before present; no standard identifier is present in the deposit at all.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Cannot be written usefully, because the join would supply the occurrence records on one side and this paper supplies only a model's prediction on the other, which means the combination tests the paper's model rather than answering a new question.

controls.positive_control: None available: with no measured occurrence records in the deposit there is nothing a working model must recover.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling would be runnable in principle, but on a circular target it would only confirm the circularity.
controls.external_validation: Fossil occurrence compilations (Neotoma, published radiocarbon datasets) exist independently, but they would be the training data, not validation, since this paper deposits no measurements to validate against.

honest_claim_h3: The only claim this deposit supports is 'a neural network can reproduce the authors' Mahalanobis-distance habitat surface from the climate fields that generated it', which is a statement about curve-fitting, not about woolly rhinoceroses or about where they lived.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use past climate at a place and time to predict whether woolly rhinoceroses could live there.
plain_idea.train_on: The intended input was paleoclimate variables (temperature, precipitation, vegetation) on a 0.5 degree global grid for each of the last 500,000 years. Those predictor layers are not in the deposit; only the 720 x 360 x 501 grid of model output is, which I verified.
plain_idea.predict: A habitat suitability score from 0 to 1 for each place and time. Critically, the true answer here is not a measurement of anything: the README states it is 'derived from a Mahalanobis distance-based model' the authors fitted themselves.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Ice Age ecologists and conservation biologists want to know which refuges let cold-adapted large mammals survive climate swings, which bears on how today's cold-specialist species will fare. But this deposit cannot answer that, because it contains a conclusion rather than the evidence behind it.

more_or_better_data.why: We would have less data, not more. The deposit contains zero occurrence records, while public compilations such as Neotoma already hold fossil localities for Eurasian megafauna; the genomic side is at most 43 specimens.

confidence_score.why: There are no replicate measurements and no measurement error of any kind here, because nothing in the file was measured. A smooth deterministic surface cannot support a calibrated uncertainty estimate.

models_beatable.why: The question is meaningless in this case. The paper's Mahalanobis model reports no accuracy figure on any split, so there is no number to beat, and the 2026 deep-learning benchmark found neural networks do not beat classical species distribution models on average and do worse for data-poor species.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Three of the four conditions fail: the paper's model cannot be run as a baseline (its predictor inputs are not deposited), our model would not see what it saw, and there is no shared evaluation split because no evaluation was ever defined.

ml_idea: The project considered was a machine-learning species distribution model: predict woolly rhinoceros habitat suitability across Eurasia over 500,000 years from paleoclimate layers, with a held-out-time-period split to test whether suitability learned from one glacial cycle transfers to the next. It dies on the data: the deposit contains the suitability surface but neither the climate predictors that produced it nor the fossil occurrence records that would constitute a real measured label.

effort.compute_note: Working set and peak memory derived from the verified file size (519,460,377 bytes = 720 x 360 x 501 four-byte floats) assuming one time slice is read at a time, which standard NetCDF readers do by default. Nothing was timed, because no feature table can be built and no model was attempted.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Read the archive's README before downloading anything. One ranged HTTP request shows the sole data variable is habitat suitability 'derived from a Mahalanobis distance-based model', which kills the project in about two minutes: the label is another model's output, and the predictors behind it were never deposited.

verdict_reason: Four Part A killers fail, all verified by opening the archive rather than reading the paper. A8: the only deposited quantity is the output of the authors' own Mahalanobis-distance habitat model, so any model trained on it distils their arithmetic instead of learning biology. A2: no measured outcome column exists; fossil occurrence records and specimen tables are absent and sit behind the Science paywall. A3: the climate predictors named in the file name are not in the file, which carries only longitude, latitude, time and the single output variable. A5: the genomic side is at most 43 specimens (29 mitochondrial plus 14 nuclear genomes), far under the 400 floor, and the 93 million grid cells are a smooth surface, not independent observations. The paper is excellent paleogenomics; the deposit is figure-reproduction material, which is a different thing from a dataset.
